title: Balancing a seesaw
why: A seesaw, a spanner and a crane all turn about a point. What makes one side go down is the first idea of statics.
idea: A weight on a seesaw turns it about the pivot. How hard it turns depends on two things: how heavy it is, and how far it sits from the pivot.
Multiply them and you get its moment. When the moments on both sides are equal, the seesaw stays level.
principle: weight × distance on the left = weight × distance on the right

predict.question: You slide the 3 kg counterweight from 1 m out to 4 m. What happens?

explain: The counterweight side drops. A weight turns harder the further it sits from the pivot: at 4 m the counterweight's moment is 3 kg × 4 m = 12, against the load's 2 kg × 3 m = 6. Distance counts as much as weight.
watch: A 2 kg load sits 3 m left of the pivot. A 3 kg counterweight sits 4 m out on the right.
Each side turns the plank with weight times distance: 6 on the left, 12 on the right.
Slide the counterweight in to 1 m and it turns with only 3. Now the load wins.
At 3 m it turns with 9: closer to 6, but still too much.
Your turn: find where the counterweight balances the load.

idealised: The plank weighs nothing and sits exactly on its middle, and the weights are points at whole metres. A real plank has its own weight and a real seesaw has friction at the pivot.
